newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia local bonds seen competing with T-bills.
newsitem.headline: Russia local bonds seen competing with T-bills.

text.p: Russia's nascent market of municipal and regional bonds will be able to compete with the bigger Treasury bill market the day it becomes fully transparent and open for non-residents, market participants say.

With the average yield on the 300 trillion rouble ($52 billion) market of GKO Treasury bills and OFZ government bonds tumbling below 20 percent currently from 85-90 percent a year ago, investors are looking for more profitable investments.
"Many people see Russian regional and munibonds as an alternative to T-bills whose yields are falling," said Andrei Zaitsev, local currency domestic market dealer at ING Bank Eurasia.

Municipal bonds issued by major regions currently pay a yield of up to three percentage points over federal paper, while the most liquid farm bonds, restructured from 1996 federal agriculture credits to the regions, are yielding 25 percent.
But as farm bonds issued by smaller regions start to trade, yields could be as high as 30 percent, dealers said.

"There is a lot of money, inside Russia and abroad, which is ready to come to this market," said Sergei Vasilyev, head of debt at International Company for Finance and Investments (ICFI, or MFK in Russian) "Risks on regional debt are acceptable."
The government is keen to foster the new market but foreign investment is being held back by vague tax rules and strict controls on non-resident activities.
Non-residents cannot trade regional bonds through the special S accounts they use for government securities, and there are limits on the use of other accounts, ING's Zaitsev said.
"Besides, even the issue of T-bill taxation is unclear, to say nothing about regional papers," he added.
For this reason some non-residents prefer to trade regional bonds through off-shore units or via derivatives and other structured products such as repos.

Russia set up a programme in June for regions to issue bonds to pay 7.7 trillion roubles in defaulted 1996 agricultural credits owed to the federal government. It also intends to restructure five trillion roubles of 1995 arrears.
Farm bonds are traded on the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX), the main floor for government securities trading, and an important currency trading exchange.
MICEX said on Thursday it also plans to start trading municipal bonds of four regions, apart from those of Moscow region and Tatarstan, which are already handled by the exchange.

The finance ministry sells discount farm bonds with 10 percent coupons and one, two and three-year maturities twice a week on behalf of different regions, but demand varies widely, depending on which of the 70 regions is selling, dealers said.
Investors, especially from other ex-Soviet republics, are also looking at municipal bonds issued by the regions directly.

Russia's second city, St Petersburg, has been issuing its own municipal bonds for over two years and has set up an efficient secondary market, dealers said. The current volume of bonds is 3.9 trillion roubles nominal.

"The bonds are as attractive as T-bills, and track their yields closely. Non-residents, mainly from the Baltic states, are working through Russian banks," said Dmitry Ivanter, chief dealer for Petersburg bonds at the issue's general agent, AVK.
Sverdlovsk, the region in Russia's Urals around the industrial city of Yekaterinburg, has also detected foreign interest for its OKO municipal bonds, of which 195 billion roubles have been issued.

"No foreign company is an authorised dealer for the bonds but as far as we know, companies from the Baltic republics were buying them in tiny amounts," said Galina Zakharova, head of securities at Sverdlovsk's finance department.
But the key to opening up the market is giving foreigner's access, said ICFI's Vasilyev.

ICFI, trade agent for the finance ministry in the farm bonds, believes the way to enlarge the market is to allow non-residents to use S accounts for trading both government and local securities, he said.
"The market will wake up if it becomes possible to trade them the same way as T-bills are traded," Vasilyev said.
"The time has come for regional paper. If access is easier, big funds will come. They will not be shifted from T-bills, it will be new money."
($1=5,787 roubles)
